## Sertraline during lactation: evidence brief

**Evidence status:** Sertraline identity was matched exactly. The retrieved material is partial and is not a safety verdict. The lactation evidence should not be generalized to pregnancy or to every sertraline formulation. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json) [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed reports that a midwife observed **six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a separate case, one mother reported increased milk supply during a temporary interruption and decreased supply after restarting. The retrieved passage does not establish causation or provide the exact elapsed time between these events. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed also discusses galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia reports, including reports in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients. Their applicability to lactation is not established by this extract. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure in milk

The retrieved LactMed record reported the following **milk concentrations**:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, in a pooled analysis involving 15 mothers. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a 24-hour milk-sampling study of 26 breastfeeding women: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**); norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In four mothers sampled at two months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; sampling times were random. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, milk levels measured on three days at random times averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One additional milk concentration was reported as **29 mcg/L**; the two sampling times were not stated. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The returned extract did **not** include an infant-level concentration excerpt. Infant-level specimen information and measurements are therefore missing from this extract; this does not establish that no infant-level measurements exist. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

- LactMed reports one four-month-old infant with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously. The retrieved passage reports the maternal sertraline exposure but does not establish causation. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a group of 26 breastfed infants, the source reported no detectable acute adverse reactions attributed to sertraline in breast milk. The source population and study context should be reviewed in the complete record. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of 14 mothers and their breastfed infants, whole-blood serotonin was measured after 6–16 weeks of maternal therapy. Infant serotonin averaged **227 mcg/L before** and **224 mcg/L after** maternal therapy. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are separate study or case findings. The retrieved extract does not establish that the reported infant events were caused by sertraline, and it does not provide a complete study count. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Product-label context

The selected label was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, DailyMed effective date **November 5, 2026**. It is one selected product label, not every sertraline formulation. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and its metabolites in human milk. It reports a pooled analysis of 53 mother–infant pairs in which exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels equal to 2% of maternal serum levels, with a reported range of 0%–15%; the label states that no adverse reactions were observed in those infants. The label also states that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The returned label included an adverse-reactions section for the person taking the medicine. Expected sections for warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions were missing from the returned extract; missing sections are retrieval limitations, not evidence that those sections contain no information. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### FAERS report-only context

The retrieved FAERS query covered reports matching sertraline, with the queried population not confirmed as lactating people or infants. Reported terms included nausea (**14,075**), “drug ineffective” (**13,855**), fatigue (**13,021**), headache (**11,284**), anxiety (**10,530**), diarrhoea (**10,499**), dizziness (**9,741**), and depression (**9,612**). [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)

These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes. The query has no exposure denominator, does not establish causation, and cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Literature and retrieval limitations

The PubMed search returned five records. Abstract text was retrieved for **3 of 5** requested records. No abstract text was returned for **PMID 38133585** and **PMID 32320387**; this is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. No unreturned or failed abstract lookups were reported. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)

The search was bounded rather than systematic. LactMed’s **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated in the returned extract, so this brief is not complete. The returned LactMed study count is missing in the exported data; the number of references is not a study count. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Questions to ask your clinician

- Does this evidence apply to my exact medicine, formulation, and active ingredients?
- How closely do these study populations match my lactation context, including the infant’s age and prematurity?
- Which findings measure milk or infant exposure, and which describe observed clinical outcomes?
- Which uncertainties or missing evidence are most relevant to my situation?
- How should my clinical needs and the infant’s health be considered together?
- What follow-up information should we discuss?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states: **Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.**

items.text: Sertraline is metabolized to norsertraline (desmethylsertraline), which has antidepressant activity of about 10% that of sertraline.

In a pooled analysis of serum levels from published studies and 4 unpublished cases, the authors found that 15 mothers taking an average daily dosage of 83 mg (range 25 to 200 mg) had an average breastmilk sertraline level of 45 mcg/L (range 7 to 207 mcg/L).[1] Using the average dosage and milk level data from this paper, an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an estimated 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage of sertraline.

Twenty-six women who were an average of 15.8 weeks postpartum (range 5 to 36 weeks) and receiving an average of 124 mg sertraline daily for at least 14 days for severe depression were studied while breastfeeding with extensive milk and serum sampling over a 24-hour period.
All milk samples had detectable sertraline (average 129 mcg/L; range 11 to 938 mcg/L) and norsertraline (average 258 mcg/L; range 20 to 1498 mcg/L).

sections.pregnancy: Pregnancy Exposure Registry There is a pregnancy exposure registry that monitors pregnancy outcomes in women exposed to antidepressants during pregnancy. Healthcare providers should encourage patients to enroll by calling the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants at 1-866-961-2388 or visiting online at https://womensmentalhealth.org/research/pregnancyregistry/antidepressants. Risk Summary Based on data from published observational studies, exposure to SSRIs, particularly in the month before delivery, has been associated with less than 2-fold increase in the risk of postpartum hemorrhage [see Warnings and Precautions (5.3)and Clinical Considerations]. Overall, available published epidemiologic studies of pregnant women exposed to sertraline in the first trimester suggest no difference in major birth defect risk compared to the background rate for major birth defects in comparator populations. ### Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed reports that a midwife observed **six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a separate case, one mother reported increased milk supply during a temporary interruption and decreased supply after restarting. The retrieved passage does not establish causation or provide the exact elapsed time between these events. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed also discusses galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia reports, including reports in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients. Their applicability to lactation is not established by this extract. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure in milk

The retrieved LactMed record reported the following **milk concentrations**:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, in a pooled analysis involving 15 mothers. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a 24-hour milk-sampling study of 26 breastfeeding women: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**); norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In four mothers sampled at two months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; sampling times were random. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, milk levels measured on three days at random times averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One additional milk concentration was reported as **29 mcg/L**; the two sampling times were not stated. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

- LactMed reports one four-month-old infant with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously. The retrieved passage reports the maternal sertraline exposure but does not establish causation. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

## Sertraline during lactation: evidence brief

**Evidence status:** Sertraline identity was matched exactly. The retrieved material is partial and is not a safety verdict. The lactation evidence should not be generalized to pregnancy or to every sertraline formulation. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json) [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Effect on the lactating person

- LactMed reports that a midwife observed **six patients who reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline**; administered amounts were not reported. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a separate case, one mother reported increased milk supply during a temporary interruption and decreased supply after restarting. The retrieved passage does not establish causation or provide the exact elapsed time between these events. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- LactMed also discusses galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia reports, including reports in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients. Their applicability to lactation is not established by this extract. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Measured exposure in milk

The retrieved LactMed record reported the following **milk concentrations**:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, in a pooled analysis involving 15 mothers. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a 24-hour milk-sampling study of 26 breastfeeding women: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**); norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In four mothers sampled at two months postpartum, average milk concentrations were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; sampling times were random. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, milk levels measured on three days at random times averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One additional milk concentration was reported as **29 mcg/L**; the two sampling times were not stated. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The returned extract did **not** include an infant-level concentration excerpt. Infant-level specimen information and measurements are therefore missing from this extract; this does not establish that no infant-level measurements exist. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

- LactMed reports one four-month-old infant with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and agitation that resolved spontaneously. The retrieved passage reports the maternal sertraline exposure but does not establish causation. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a group of 26 breastfed infants, the source reported no detectable acute adverse reactions attributed to sertraline in breast milk. The source population and study context should be reviewed in the complete record. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of 14 mothers and their breastfed infants, whole-blood serotonin was measured after 6–16 weeks of maternal therapy. Infant serotonin averaged **227 mcg/L before** and **224 mcg/L after** maternal therapy. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are separate study or case findings. The retrieved extract does not establish that the reported infant events were caused by sertraline, and it does not provide a complete study count. [S55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Product-label context

The selected label was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, DailyMed effective date **November 5, 2026**. It is one selected product label, not every sertraline formulation. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and its metabolites in human milk. It reports a pooled analysis of 53 mother–infant pairs in which exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels equal to 2% of maternal serum levels, with a reported range of 0%–15%; the label states that no adverse reactions were observed in those infants. The label also states that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The returned label included an adverse-reactions section for the person taking the medicine. Expected sections for warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions were missing from the returned extract; missing sections are retrieval limitations, not evidence that those sections contain no information. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

Reported terms included nausea (**14,075**), “drug ineffective” (**13,855**), fatigue (**13,021**), headache (**11,284**), anxiety (**10,530**), diarrhoea (**10,499**), dizziness (**9,741**), and depression (**9,612**). The query has no exposure denominator, does not establish causation, and cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline.
